questions.questionMd: Given two k-gram sets A and B, which expression correctly computes their Jaccard similarity?
questions.explanationMd: Jaccard similarity is the size of the intersection divided by the size of the union of two sets.

questions.questionMd: What is the recommended skip pointer interval for a postings list of length 400?
questions.explanationMd: A common heuristic is to place about √P skips for a postings list of length P, so √400 = 20.

questions.questionMd: Which 1960s development is credited as the first systematic, reproducible evaluation of IR systems, establishing the methodology of using test collections and relevance judgments?

options.text: The introduction of Luhn's automatic keyword extraction
The launch of MEDLARS at the National Library of Medicine
The SMART system developed by Salton at Cornell
The Cranfield experiments

questions.explanationMd: The Cranfield experiments established reusable test collections with queries and relevance judgments for systematic IR evaluation.

questions.questionMd: The NLTK English stopword list contains approximately how many words, and what is the approximate size of Lucene's default stopword list?

options.text: 179 words in NLTK and approximately 179 in Lucene
500 words in NLTK and approximately 100 in Lucene
33 words in NLTK and approximately 179 in Lucene
179 words in NLTK and approximately 33 in Lucene

questions.explanationMd: The lecture contrast is that NLTK's English stopword list is much larger than Lucene's default English stopword list.

questions.questionMd: In the Average Precision formula `AP = (1/R) × Σ P@k`, what does the summation run over?

options.text: Only the rank positions k where the retrieved document is relevant
All rank positions from 1 to the total number of retrieved documents
All positions where the retrieved document is irrelevant, as a penalty term
The top-k positions specified by the evaluation cutoff

questions.explanationMd: Average Precision averages precision values only at the ranks where a relevant document is retrieved.

questions.questionMd: A medical literature search system is designed to ensure clinicians find every relevant study on a drug interaction. Which evaluation metric is most appropriate?

options.text: P@5, because clinicians typically only read the first five results returned
NDCG@10, because graded relevance most accurately reflects a clinician's document preferences
MAP, because it rewards retrieving all relevant documents and penalises any that are missed
MRR, because clinicians only need to find the single most authoritative study for each query

questions.explanationMd: MAP evaluates performance across relevant documents and is suitable when recall of all relevant studies matters.

questions.questionMd: Given the ranked list `R, I, I, R, R` where R = relevant and I = irrelevant, what is the Average Precision (AP)?
questions.explanationMd: Relevant documents occur at ranks 1, 4, and 5. AP = (1/3)(1/1 + 2/4 + 3/5) = 0.700.

questions.questionMd: In the Vector Space Model, why are document vectors described as sparse?

options.text: Document vectors are sparse because only the top-k highest-weighted terms are stored to save memory
Vectors are sparse because cosine normalization sets most small weights to zero during L2 normalization
Sparsity arises because IDF values are rounded to zero for any term with document frequency above a threshold
Most vocabulary terms do not appear in any given document

questions.explanationMd: A document usually contains only a small subset of the full vocabulary, so most vector dimensions are zero.

questions.questionMd: Lucene uses a Finite State Transducer (FST) as its term dictionary structure. What property makes the FST particularly well-suited for this role?

options.text: It is a hash map that maps each term to its document frequency, enabling O(1) IDF lookups during scoring.
It is a compact, memory-efficient graph that supports O(len) prefix and suffix lookups on the sorted term list.
It uses a B-tree structure to guarantee O(log n) insertion time when new terms are added to a mutable segment.
It stores postings lists in columnar format so that aggregations can be computed without loading all term data into RAM.

questions.explanationMd: Lucene's FST compactly represents a sorted term dictionary and enables efficient term lookup and prefix-style traversal.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture notes, which of the following statements about BM25 scores is correct?

options.text: BM25 scores are calibrated probabilities that sum to 1 across all documents for a given query
BM25 scores are symmetric, meaning the score for query Q against document D equals the score for D against Q
BM25 scores always fall within the range [0, 1] because the IDF component is bounded by log(N)
BM25 scores are ordinal relevance estimates and should not be compared across different queries

questions.explanationMd: BM25 scores are ranking scores for a particular query; their absolute values are not calibrated probabilities and are not directly comparable across queries.

questions.questionMd: After intersecting k-gram postings to resolve a wildcard query, why is a mandatory post-filtering step required?

options.text: The k-gram intersection can only retrieve terms from a single partition of the vocabulary at a time
K-gram matching is a necessary but not sufficient condition
K-gram postings lists are unsorted, so the intersection result contains duplicate terms
Post-filtering converts k-gram integer IDs back into human-readable vocabulary terms

questions.explanationMd: A term may contain the required k-grams but still fail the original wildcard pattern, so candidates must be checked against the wildcard itself.

questions.questionMd: In the three-stage spelling correction pipeline, what is the primary purpose of the Jaccard similarity filtering stage?

options.text: To eliminate most implausible candidates cheaply before the expensive edit distance computation
To rank the final correction suggestions by their phonetic similarity to the misspelled word
To apply context-sensitive correction by comparing candidates against a bigram language model
To build the initial candidate set by finding all vocabulary terms sharing at least one k-gram

questions.explanationMd: Jaccard filtering is a cheap candidate-pruning step before more expensive edit-distance scoring.

questions.questionMd: Which query structure correctly follows the best practice for using the NOT operator?

options.text: Replace every NOT operand with an equivalent OR over all other terms
Perform an AND merge first to reduce the candidate set, then apply NOT to the result
Lead the query with NOT to eliminate irrelevant documents before any AND merge
Apply NOT to the largest postings list to maximize the pruning effect

questions.explanationMd: NOT is best applied after positive terms have restricted the candidate set; leading with NOT can require scanning a very large complement.

questions.questionMd: In the positional index approach to phrase queries, what is the role of the first phase?

options.text: It verifies that query terms appear at consecutive positions in each document
It uses an AND merge
It resolves wildcard patterns into concrete vocabulary terms using the k-gram index
It applies Jaccard similarity to rank candidate documents by term overlap

questions.explanationMd: Phrase query processing first finds candidate documents containing all terms, usually by an AND merge; positional checks come afterward.

questions.questionMd: Why does the smoothed IDF formula `log(N / (df + 1)) + 1` add 1 to the denominator?

options.text: To ensure that every term receives an IDF value greater than 1 regardless of collection size
To make very common terms receive a higher IDF than they would under the standard formula
To bring the IDF range into alignment with the range produced by log-TF
To prevent division by zero when a term has never appeared in any document in the collection

questions.explanationMd: Adding 1 to df avoids division by zero for unseen terms and makes the formula numerically safe.

questions.questionMd: Which formula correctly defines the F1 score in terms of Precision (P) and Recall (R)?

options.text: PR / (P + R)
2PR / (P + R)

questions.explanationMd: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: `2PR / (P + R)`.

questions.questionMd: An OpenSearch index is created with 3 primary shards. After the index goes into production, the team finds that data has grown and they need more shards. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Use the Shard Split API to divide each existing primary shard into smaller shards without reindexing.
Increase the replica count, which automatically redistributes documents across more shards.
Create a new index with the desired shard count and reindex all documents into it.
Update the index settings at runtime to increase the number of primary shards.

questions.explanationMd: The number of primary shards is effectively fixed for an index; changing it typically requires creating a new index and reindexing data.

questions.questionMd: In Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG), relevance scores are divided by the log base-2 of `(rank + 1)`. What user behavior does this logarithmic discount model?

options.text: Users prefer documents that are only marginally relevant at high ranks over highly relevant documents at low ranks
Users read results in random order, so position should have no effect on contribution
The discount penalizes systems that retrieve more than k documents, keeping result sets short
User attention diminishes at lower ranks, so a relevant document at rank 10 is worth less than one at rank 1

questions.explanationMd: DCG discounts lower-ranked results because users are less likely to inspect or value results far down the ranking.

questions.questionMd: According to SMART notation, which formula defines the logarithmic TF variant (symbol `l`) for a term with a non-zero count?

options.text: tf / (1 + log(tf))
1 + log(tf)
log(tf) - 1

questions.explanationMd: In SMART notation, logarithmic term frequency weighting is commonly defined as `1 + log(tf)` for tf > 0.

questions.questionMd: Which organisation established TREC (Text REtrieval Conference) in 1992 to provide shared benchmarks for IR evaluation?

options.text: DARPA (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency)
ACM (Association for Computing Machinery)
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology)
IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers)

questions.explanationMd: TREC is organized by NIST and provides shared evaluation tasks, datasets, and benchmarks for IR systems.

questions.questionMd: In a positional index, what specific information is stored for each term-document pair that is absent from a basic inverted index?

options.text: The document frequency of the term across the entire corpus
The term frequency of each token normalized by document length
The positions (offsets) of each token occurrence within the document
The byte offset of the document in the original corpus file

questions.explanationMd: A positional index stores the positions of term occurrences, enabling phrase and proximity queries.

questions.questionMd: Which sequence correctly represents the order of the seven stages in the standard IR pipeline introduced in Week 1?

options.text: Preprocess → Crawl → Index → Rank → Query Processing → Present → Evaluate
Crawl → Index → Preprocess → Query Processing → Evaluate → Rank → Present
Query Processing → Crawl → Preprocess → Index → Rank → Evaluate → Present
Crawl → Preprocess → Index → Query Processing → Rank → Present → Evaluate

questions.explanationMd: The standard flow first gathers and prepares documents, builds the index, processes queries, ranks and presents results, then evaluates performance.

questions.questionMd: Case folding converts "Apple" to "apple" during normalization. According to the lecture, which specific example demonstrates that lowercasing is NOT always a safe operation?

options.text: "Apple" (company name) vs. "apple" (the fruit) carry different meanings
"running" and "running" should always be treated as the same term
Accent folding should always be performed before case folding
"NASA" should always be lowercased to "nasa" for consistency

questions.explanationMd: Lowercasing can erase meaningful distinctions, such as a proper noun brand name versus a common noun.

questions.questionMd: A corpus contains 1000 documents, and the term "quasar" appears in exactly 50 of them. Applying the formula `IDF(t) = log(N / df(t))`, what is the IDF of "quasar"?
questions.explanationMd: N/df = 1000/50 = 20, so the IDF is `log(20)`, approximately 3.0 using natural log.

questions.questionMd: Which specific problem motivated the development of the BM25F variant?

options.text: Standard BM25 cannot handle multi-word queries because it sums scores term by term, a limitation BM25F overcomes
Standard BM25 requires all documents in the collection to have the same length, which BM25F relaxes with per-document normalization
Standard BM25 treats a document as a single flat text field
Standard BM25 produces negative IDF values for terms with very high document frequency, which BM25F corrects

questions.explanationMd: BM25F extends BM25 to handle multiple document fields, such as title, body, and anchor text, rather than treating the document as one flat field.

questions.questionMd: A developer uses `SELECT * FROM papers WHERE abstract LIKE '%heart attack%'` to find cardiology research. What is the most significant limitation of this approach compared to an IR system?

options.text: It returns no results for documents using the synonym "myocardial infarction"
It requires a separate full-text parser before the SQL engine can execute
It cannot filter results by publication date or author name
It is slower than an inverted index for corpora with fewer than one million rows

questions.explanationMd: A literal substring search misses semantically related terms and synonyms that an IR system may handle through analysis, expansion, or ranking.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture's compression data, combining gap encoding with VB encoding on a typical postings list achieves what overall compression factor compared to storing raw int32 doc IDs?

options.text: Exactly 8× compression because VB uses 7 data bits per byte instead of 8
Less than 1.5× compression
Approximately 3–5× compression
Approximately 10–20× compression

questions.explanationMd: Gap encoding reduces the magnitude of numbers and variable-byte encoding stores small gaps compactly, often giving a few-fold compression improvement.

questions.questionMd: In Apache Lucene's segment-based architecture, what happens when a document is updated?

options.text: The existing segment is opened and the document's fields are overwritten in place.
The old document is marked as deleted and the updated version is written as a new entry.
The document is moved to a special update buffer that replaces the original segment during the next merge.
All segments containing that document are merged immediately to apply the update atomically.

questions.explanationMd: Lucene segments are immutable, so updates are implemented by deleting the old document and adding the new version.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture notes, when is the `avgdl` (average document length) statistic used by BM25 computed?

options.text: At query time by averaging the lengths of all retrieved candidate documents
Each time a new document is added to the index, `avgdl` is recomputed from scratch
Once at index construction time and stored as a collection-level statistic
Only during evaluation when comparing BM25 against TF-IDF outputs

questions.explanationMd: BM25 uses collection-level statistics such as average document length, which are computed from the indexed collection and reused during scoring.

questions.questionMd: In the text preprocessing pipeline, what is the correct order of stages?

options.text: Remove Stopwords → Tokenize → Normalize → Stem/Lemmatize → Index Terms
Tokenize → Normalize → Remove Stopwords → Stem/Lemmatize → Index Terms
Tokenize → Stem/Lemmatize → Normalize → Remove Stopwords → Index Terms
Normalize → Tokenize → Stem/Lemmatize → Remove Stopwords → Index Terms

questions.explanationMd: A typical pipeline first tokenizes text, normalizes tokens, removes stopwords, stems or lemmatizes terms, and then indexes them.

questions.questionMd: The two-pointer AND merge achieves O(m + n) time complexity only because of one crucial property of postings lists. What is that property?

options.text: Postings lists contain positional information for each document
Postings lists are stored in order of decreasing term frequency
Postings lists are stored in sorted order of document ID
Postings lists use variable-byte encoded gaps between document IDs

questions.explanationMd: Linear two-pointer intersection depends on both postings lists being sorted by document ID.

questions.questionMd: What is the core intuition behind Inverse Document Frequency (IDF) as used in TF-IDF weighting?

options.text: Terms that appear in many documents are more likely to be relevant to any query
IDF penalizes terms based on how frequently they appear within a single document
IDF increases the weight of terms that co-occur with stopwords
Terms that appear in many documents carry little discriminating information and should receive lower weights

questions.explanationMd: IDF downweights common terms because they are less useful for distinguishing relevant documents from non-relevant ones.

questions.questionMd: A term has high TF in a document but very low IDF across the collection. What does this combination indicate about the term's usefulness as a relevance signal?

options.text: The term is a strong relevance signal because high TF always dominates the combined TF-IDF weight
The term is highly informative because low IDF indicates it appears in very few documents
The term is a weak discriminator because it appears frequently in many documents
The term should be removed from the index because its combined TF-IDF weight will be exactly zero

questions.explanationMd: Low IDF means the term is common across the collection, so even frequent occurrence in one document may not strongly distinguish relevance.

questions.questionMd: On a log-log plot of term rank vs. term frequency, what shape does Zipf's Law predict?

options.text: A straight line with a slope of approximately -1
A concave curve that levels off as rank increases
An S-shaped logistic curve
A straight line with a positive slope

questions.explanationMd: Zipf's Law states frequency is roughly inversely proportional to rank, which appears as a line with slope about -1 on a log-log plot.

questions.questionMd: A term receives a high TF-IDF weight in a document when which condition holds?

options.text: The term appears rarely in that document but frequently across the overall collection
The term has a low IDF value and a high document frequency
The term appears in every document in the collection
The term appears frequently in that document but rarely across the overall collection

questions.explanationMd: High TF-IDF requires both high term frequency in the document and high IDF, meaning the term is rare across the collection.

questions.questionMd: In gap (delta) encoding of a postings list, how is the very first entry in the list stored?

options.text: As the absolute document ID, not as a gap
As a special sentinel value indicating the beginning of the list
As a gap of zero to signal the start of the list
As the difference between the first and second document IDs

questions.explanationMd: Since there is no previous document ID before the first posting, the first entry is stored directly as the absolute document ID.

questions.questionMd: A proximity query is written as `term1 /k term2`. Which condition must hold in a candidate document for it to be included in the result?

options.text: The positional difference between term1 and term2 must be at most k
The total count of term1 and term2 occurrences in the document must equal k
term1 must appear exactly k positions before term2 in every occurrence
The terms must appear in the same sentence and within k paragraphs of each other

questions.explanationMd: A proximity operator requires the two terms to occur within a maximum positional distance k.

questions.questionMd: What must a developer do in code when computing NDCG@k for a query that has no relevant documents in the collection?

options.text: Exclude that query from the evaluation and reduce Q by 1 in the MAP formula
Return 0.0 as a special-case guard, because IDCG = 0 makes the formula undefined
Return 1.0, because a system cannot be penalised for a query with no correct answers
Assign each retrieved document a relevance grade of 1 and recompute normally

questions.explanationMd: NDCG divides DCG by IDCG. If there are no relevant documents, IDCG is zero, so code must handle the undefined case explicitly.

questions.questionMd: When constructing an 11-point interpolated Precision-Recall curve, how is interpolated Precision defined at a given recall level r?

options.text: The minimum Precision across all recall levels r' > r, to represent a pessimistic bound
The Precision value recorded the first time recall r is reached during retrieval
The arithmetic mean of Precision values immediately before and after recall level r
The maximum Precision achieved at any recall level r' that is greater than or equal to r

questions.explanationMd: Interpolated precision at recall r is the maximum precision observed at any recall level r' ≥ r.

questions.questionMd: A user searches "automobile fuel efficiency" but the most relevant document uses only the phrases "car gas mileage" and "vehicle consumption". What problem does this scenario illustrate?

options.text: The precision-recall tradeoff — retrieving more documents lowers average result quality
The vocabulary mismatch problem — lexical overlap is zero despite near-identical meaning
The corpus freshness problem — the index has not been updated to include recent terminology
The stopword problem — common function words are masking the discriminating content terms

questions.explanationMd: The query and document use different words for the same concept, so exact lexical matching can fail despite semantic similarity.

questions.questionMd: Why is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test generally preferred over the paired t-test for comparing per-query AP score distributions in IR experiments?

options.text: The paired t-test requires at least 1,000 queries to produce valid results, while Wilcoxon works on any sample size
Wilcoxon is non-parametric and does not assume that per-query score differences are normally distributed
Wilcoxon is always more statistically powerful than the t-test, producing lower p-values on the same data
Wilcoxon directly optimises NDCG, making it more aligned with the evaluation objective than the t-test

questions.explanationMd: Wilcoxon is a non-parametric paired test and is useful when score differences may not satisfy normality assumptions.

questions.questionMd: A student runs a Porter stemmer and observes that both "universe" and "university" produce the stem "univers". This is an example of which failure mode?

options.text: Over-stemming, which reduces retrieval precision
Accent folding, which merges morphologically unrelated forms

questions.explanationMd: Over-stemming merges terms that should remain distinct, which can increase false matches and reduce precision.

questions.questionMd: A retrieval system returns 10 documents in response to a query. Seven of them are relevant. The corpus contains 20 relevant documents in total. What are the precision and recall values?

options.text: Precision = 0.35, Recall = 0.35
Precision = 0.7, Recall = 0.35
Precision = 0.7, Recall = 0.7
Precision = 0.35, Recall = 0.7

questions.explanationMd: Precision = relevant retrieved / retrieved = 7/10 = 0.7. Recall = relevant retrieved / total relevant = 7/20 = 0.35.

questions.questionMd: Zipf's Law states that the frequency of the r-th most common word is proportional to 1/r. If the most frequent term in a corpus appears 10,000 times, approximately how often does the 100th most frequent term appear?

options.text: Approximately 10 times
Approximately 1,000 times
Approximately 100 times
Approximately 5,000 times

questions.explanationMd: Using frequency ≈ 10000 / r, the 100th term appears about 10000 / 100 = 100 times.

questions.questionMd: Which stemmer described in the lectures is characterized as the most aggressive, producing the smallest vocabulary but the highest over-stemming error rate?

options.text: WordNet lemmatizer
Porter
Lancaster
Snowball

questions.explanationMd: The Lancaster stemmer is generally more aggressive than Porter or Snowball, often reducing vocabulary size but risking over-stemming.

questions.questionMd: What is the key architectural difference between the BSBI and SPIMI index construction algorithms?

options.text: BSBI writes sorted postings directly to disk, while SPIMI keeps all postings in RAM permanently
BSBI requires a global term-to-integer mapping across all blocks, while SPIMI does not
SPIMI sorts all term-document pairs before writing any block to disk, while BSBI does not
BSBI is designed for single-pass processing, while SPIMI requires multiple passes over the corpus

questions.explanationMd: BSBI uses termID pairs and therefore needs a global term-to-ID mapping; SPIMI builds term dictionaries dynamically per block.

questions.questionMd: System A has MAP = 0.42 and System B has MAP = 0.43. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test yields p = 0.21. What is the correct conclusion?

options.text: System A is preferred because p > 0.05 confirms its stability across queries
The difference is not statistically significant
The test is invalid because the MAP difference is smaller than the p-value
System B is statistically and practically superior because it has a higher MAP score

questions.explanationMd: With p = 0.21, the difference does not meet a typical 0.05 significance threshold, so the observed MAP difference is not statistically significant.

questions.questionMd: In the Boolean retrieval model, what does a query return?

options.text: A ranked list of documents sorted by relevance score
A set of document IDs sorted by term frequency
A probability distribution over matching documents
A set of document IDs with no ordering or relevance scores

questions.explanationMd: Boolean retrieval returns an unordered set of documents that satisfy the Boolean expression, not a ranked list.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following is a fundamental limitation of Boolean retrieval that motivates the move to ranked retrieval?

options.text: Boolean retrieval requires all query terms to be stemmed before matching
Boolean retrieval is unable to handle OR operators between query terms
Boolean retrieval cannot use an inverted index to look up postings lists
A document matching 3 out of 4 query terms is assigned one matching 0 terms

questions.explanationMd: Boolean retrieval has binary matching: documents either satisfy the query or not, so partial matches may receive no credit.

questions.questionMd: A ranked list has graded relevance scores `[3, 1, 0, 2, 1]` at ranks 1 through 5. What is the approximate DCG@5?

options.text: 7.00, computed by summing the raw relevance grades 3+1+0+2+1
2.50, computed as the arithmetic mean of the five relevance grades
3.00, because only the first rank contributes and its grade is 3

questions.explanationMd: DCG discounts relevance by log2(rank+1): 3/1 + 1/log2(3) + 0/log2(4) + 2/log2(5) + 1/log2(6) ≈ 4.879.

questions.questionMd: A developer indexes a document in OpenSearch and immediately issues a search query but does not find the new document. Which concept best explains this behavior?

options.text: Near-real-time search requires a refresh before newly indexed documents become searchable.
The document must be replicated to all replica shards before it can appear in search results.

questions.explanationMd: OpenSearch is near-real-time: newly indexed documents generally become searchable after a refresh exposes them to search.

questions.questionMd: After applying the full preprocessing pipeline (tokenize → lowercase → stopword removal → Porter stemming) to the input "The astronauts ORBITING the International Space Station", which term in the output best illustrates a known over-stemming problem?

options.text: "space" produced from "Space"
"intern" produced from "International"
"station" produced from "Station"
"astronaut" produced from "astronauts"

questions.explanationMd: Stemming "International" to "intern" can merge it with unrelated concepts, illustrating over-stemming.

questions.questionMd: In TREC relevance judging, Cohen's κ values typically fall between 0.6 and 0.8. What does this imply about IR evaluation?

options.text: Annotators disagree so frequently that per-query results are unreliable and should be discarded
Agreement is nearly perfect, so evaluation results can be treated as ground truth without reservation
The κ range shows that automated relevance labeling is more reliable than human judgment
There is substantial but imperfect agreement among assessors.

questions.explanationMd: A κ range of about 0.6-0.8 is usually interpreted as substantial agreement, but not perfect agreement.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following best explains why simple whitespace tokenization is insufficient for production search systems?

options.text: It always produces more tokens than a regex-based tokenizer would for the same input
It requires an external dictionary to identify valid word boundaries
It is too slow for large corpora because it scans the entire text character by character
It fails to handle contractions, possessives, URLs, and hyphenated expressions correctly

questions.explanationMd: Production tokenizers must handle punctuation, contractions, URLs, hyphenation, and other cases that simple whitespace splitting misses.

questions.questionMd: Variable-byte (VB) encoding uses a continuation bit within each byte. What does a continuation bit value of 1 (the top bit set) indicate in VB encoding?

options.text: This byte encodes a negative gap and should be subtracted
This byte marks the boundary between two separate encoded numbers
This is the last (terminal) byte of the current encoded number
This byte is a continuation byte and more bytes follow for the current number

questions.explanationMd: In the convention used in the lecture, a top bit of 1 marks the final byte of the current variable-byte encoded number.

questions.questionMd: Why is leading a query with a NOT operation alone considered poor practice?

options.text: It can only be applied after an OR merge has been completed
It requires building a secondary inverted index from scratch at query time
It requires scanning the entire corpus to find all document IDs not in the negated list
It produces the same result as an AND query but takes longer to parse

questions.explanationMd: A leading NOT query requires computing the complement of a postings list, which can involve the full document universe.

questions.questionMd: In Boolean retrieval, an OR query between two terms produces results by applying which set operation to their postings lists?

options.text: Set intersection — documents containing both terms simultaneously
Set difference — documents containing the first term but not the second
Set complement — all documents not containing either term
Set union — documents containing either term or both

questions.explanationMd: Boolean OR corresponds to the union of postings lists: documents containing either term, including those containing both.
